lessonTitle: Gram-Negative Pathogens: Enteric Bacilli, Pseudomonas, Endotoxin and Neisseria

blocks.text: A 19-year-old university student wakes with a headache, fever and a few pinpoint haemorrhages on his legs that spread to purple patches within hours. His blood cultures will grow a pink diplococcus. Gram-negative bacteria cause some of the fastest, most dangerous infections in medicine, and the culprit is often not the organism itself but a lipid in its outer membrane.

blocks.markdown: Gram-negative pathogens have an outer membrane whose outer leaflet is **lipopolysaccharide (LPS)**. LPS has three parts: the **O antigen** (variable polysaccharide chain, basis of serotyping), a core oligosaccharide, and **lipid A**, the embedded, conserved lipid that is the **endotoxin**. This unit covers the enteric Gram-negative bacilli and *Pseudomonas* (common causes of urinary tract infection and bacteraemia), the role of endotoxin in septic shock, and the two pathogenic *Neisseria* species.

blocks.markdown: **Urinary infection and bacteraemia.** Most urinary tract infections ascend from the bowel flora through the urethra to the bladder (cystitis) and sometimes the kidney (pyelonephritis). *E. coli* is most frequent, followed by *Klebsiella*, *Proteus* and others; adhesive pili allow attachment to urothelium. Bacteria can enter the blood from the urinary tract (urosepsis), the gut or the biliary tree; the Gram-negative bacilli most often isolated in bacteraemia are *E. coli*, *Klebsiella* and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. *Proteus* splits urea to ammonia, raising urine pH and promoting struvite stone formation.

blocks.title: Endotoxin
blocks.text: Endotoxin is the lipid A component of lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane. It is released when bacteria die or lyse (and in small amounts during growth) and stimulates the host innate immune system through binding by lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and CD14 to the TLR4/MD-2 receptor complex.

blocks.markdown: **Endotoxin and septic shock.** Activation of TLR4 on macrophages and endothelium triggers release of **tumour necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-1 and interleukin-6**. These cause fever, widespread **vasodilatation** (nitric oxide), increased **capillary permeability**, neutrophil activation and activation of coagulation, which can lead to **disseminated intravascular coagulation**. The result is falling vascular resistance and effective blood volume, so blood pressure falls despite a normal or high cardiac output early on: **septic shock**. Small amounts of endotoxin are beneficial (they trigger defence); large amounts overwhelm the response. The effect does not depend on the organism being alive.

blocks.caption: Mean arterial pressure (mmHg) from systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP) pressure; an approximation

blocks.title: Calculating mean arterial pressure in shock
blocks.prompt: A patient with Gram-negative bacteraemia has blood pressure 90/50 mmHg. Calculate the mean arterial pressure.
blocks.answer: About 63 mmHg, reflecting reduced vascular tone from endotoxin-driven vasodilatation.

blocks.markdown: ***Neisseria*.** These are Gram-negative **diplococci** (kidney-bean shaped, pairs facing each other), oxidase-positive, aerobic. They are fastidious and grow on chocolate agar. ***N. meningitidis*** has a **polysaccharide capsule** (serogroups such as A, B, C, W and Y), is carried in the nasopharynx of a proportion of healthy people, and spreads by respiratory droplets. It ferments glucose and maltose. It causes **meningitis** and **meningococcaemia** (fulminant sepsis with a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash; massive endotoxin release can cause adrenal haemorrhage in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome and DIC). Complement deficiency and asplenia increase risk. ***N. gonorrhoeae*** has no capsule, ferments glucose only, is sexually transmitted and causes **urethritis, cervicitis** (and ascending pelvic inflammatory disease), **ophthalmia neonatorum** from vertical transmission and, less often, disseminated infection with arthritis. Pili undergo antigenic variation, so natural infection does not give lasting immunity.

blocks.title: Attack rate in close contacts
blocks.prompt: After a case of meningococcal disease in a dormitory, 3 of 120 close contacts develop disease in the following fortnight. Calculate the attack rate in close contacts.

steps.text: Attack rate = number who become ill divided by number exposed.

blocks.answer: 2.5%, far above the population risk, which is why close contacts are offered prophylaxis.

items: E. coli: commonest cause of urinary tract infection and a major cause of bacteraemia.
Proteus: urease, alkaline urine, struvite stones.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: oxidase-positive, hospital-acquired and burns, blue-green pigment.
Lipid A: TLR4 activation, TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, vasodilatation, DIC.
N. meningitidis: capsule, meningitis and purpuric sepsis; N. gonorrhoeae: urethritis, cervicitis, PID.

blocks.title: Endotoxin is the link
blocks.text: Different Gram-negative organisms and different sites of infection converge on the same shock syndrome because they share lipid A, and the host response, not direct toxicity, produces most of the harm.

blocks.title: Do not confuse
blocks.text: Endotoxin is not a secreted protein exotoxin. Both Neisseria species are Gram-negative diplococci and oxidase-positive; differentiate them by site, capsule and sugar fermentation. Antibiotic lysis of bacteria can transiently increase endotoxin release.

points: E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus and Pseudomonas are major Gram-negative causes of urinary infection and bacteraemia.
Lipid A of LPS is endotoxin; via TLR4 it triggers cytokines, vasodilatation, capillary leak and DIC leading to septic shock.
N. meningitidis: capsule, nasopharyngeal carriage, meningitis and purpuric septicaemia.
N. gonorrhoeae: no capsule, sexually transmitted, urethritis, cervicitis, PID and ophthalmia neonatorum.

questions.stem: Which organism is the commonest cause of community urinary tract infection?

distractorRationale.b: N. meningitidis causes meningitis and septicaemia.
distractorRationale.c: Pseudomonas is more important in hospital-acquired infection.

questions.explanation: E. coli from the bowel flora ascends the urethra and adheres to urothelium by pili. It is the single most common cause of both lower and upper urinary tract infection.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has recurrent urinary infections, alkaline urine (pH 8) and a staghorn calculus. Which organism is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: urease splits urea, raising pH and promoting struvite.
distractorRationale.c: N. gonorrhoeae causes genital infection, not struvite stones.
distractorRationale.d: S. pyogenes causes pharyngitis and skin infection.

questions.explanation: Proteus mirabilis produces urease, converting urea to ammonia, which raises urine pH and precipitates struvite. This also explains the staghorn stone, which harbours organisms and prolongs infection.

questions.stem: Which component of Gram-negative bacteria is responsible for the endotoxin effect in septic shock?

distractorRationale.b: Teichoic acids are in Gram-positive walls.
distractorRationale.c: Flagellin is not the classical endotoxin.
distractorRationale.d: Endotoxin is a structural component, not a secreted protein toxin.

questions.explanation: Lipid A is the conserved, bioactive part of LPS. Binding to TLR4 on macrophages triggers release of cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes how endotoxin produces hypotension?

options.text: Lipid A binds TLR4, macrophages release TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6, causing vasodilatation and capillary leak with a fall in blood pressure
Lipid A binds and blocks acetylcholine receptors, causing vasodilatation
Lipid A directly destroys cardiac muscle, reducing stroke volume only
Lipid A inhibits protein synthesis in endothelial cells, causing vasoconstriction

questions.correctOptionText: Lipid A binds TLR4, macrophages release TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6, causing vasodilatation and capillary leak with a fall in blood pressure

distractorRationale.b: This is not the mechanism of endotoxin.
distractorRationale.c: Direct cardiac destruction is not the main mechanism.
distractorRationale.d: Endotoxin causes vasodilatation rather than vasoconstriction.

questions.explanation: The harm comes from the host response to lipid A. Cytokines and nitric oxide cause vasodilatation and increased permeability, reducing effective circulating volume.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has purulent urethral discharge and dysuria. Gram stain of the discharge shows Gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils; the isolate ferments glucose but not maltose. Which organism is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: N. meningitidis ferments maltose as well as glucose and is not a usual cause of urethritis.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: intracellular diplococci in urethral pus, glucose only.
distractorRationale.d: Pseudomonas is a bacillus and does not ferment sugars.

questions.explanation: Gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils in urethral discharge indicate gonococcal urethritis. Fermenting glucose but not maltose distinguishes N. gonorrhoeae from N. meningitidis.

questions.stem: A patient with Gram-negative septic shock has a blood pressure of 78/42 mmHg. Using MAP = (SBP + 2 x DBP) / 3, calculate the mean arterial pressure in mmHg.
questions.explanation: MAP = (78 + 2 x 42) / 3 = (78 + 84) / 3 = 162 / 3 = 54 mmHg. This low value reflects endotoxin-driven vasodilatation and reduced perfusion pressure.

questions.stem: In a carriage survey, nasopharyngeal swabs are taken from 300 healthy students and Neisseria meningitidis is isolated from 36. Calculate the carriage prevalence as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Prevalence = carriers / people sampled = 36 / 300 = 0.12, or 12%. Many healthy people carry the organism harmlessly, so disease arises only in a few, which is why carriage is important in transmission.

questions.stem: Name three Gram-negative bacilli that commonly cause urinary tract infection or bacteraemia and give one distinguishing feature of each.
markingGuide: Escherichia coli: commonest cause of UTI; lactose fermenter; pili adhere to urothelium
Klebsiella pneumoniae: lactose fermenter with mucoid capsule
Proteus mirabilis: urease, alkaline urine, struvite stones, swarming
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: oxidase-positive, non-lactose fermenter, hospital-acquired infection, blue-green pigment
Source of organisms: bowel flora ascending via the urethra or entering the blood from gut, biliary tree or urinary tract
questions.explanation: Each organism has a recognisable feature that links it to its clinical niche. Knowing these allows laboratory and clinical reasoning.

questions.stem: Explain how lipopolysaccharide endotoxin leads to septic shock, starting from the bacterial structure.
markingGuide: LPS in outer leaflet of Gram-negative outer membrane; lipid A is the endotoxin
Released on lysis or growth; binds LBP, CD14 and TLR4/MD-2 on macrophages and endothelium
Release of TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6
Vasodilatation (nitric oxide) and increased capillary permeability reduce vascular resistance and effective volume
Coagulation activation and DIC; result is hypotension and organ hypoperfusion (septic shock)
questions.explanation: The sequence runs from the bacterial structure to host cytokines to the haemodynamic effects. Marking should reward each link in this chain.

questions.stem: Compare Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in terms of capsule, route of transmission and clinical syndromes.
markingGuide: N. meningitidis: capsule; nasopharyngeal carriage; respiratory droplets; meningitis and septicaemia with purpuric rash
N. gonorrhoeae: no capsule; sexual and vertical transmission
N. gonorrhoeae syndromes: urethritis, cervicitis, PID, ophthalmia neonatorum, disseminated infection
Sugar fermentation: meningitidis ferments glucose and maltose; gonorrhoeae glucose only
questions.explanation: The two species differ in capsule, niche and disease. Identification depends on site and biochemistry.
